eliyah_rabbah.en:
[1] Until six hours, etc. This includes remaining without food for the sake of a fast, for even one hour is prohibited (Maharil). Accordingly, some communities act improperly when they fast on Shabbos until midday because of decrees against the community (Magen Avraham).
[2] [Levush] Or he prays, etc. Therefore, those prayer leaders who prolong melodies and do not leave the synagogue until after six hours do not act properly, especially in winter, and all the more so on Yom Tov. Rosh Hashanah is an exception, when this should not be prevented, as Bach and Yam Shel Shlomo, Beitzah 2:4, write, although the latter concludes that when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbos it is prohibited. Magen Avraham in siman 157 justifies the practice of sometimes prolonging prayer on Shabbos and Yom Tov by counting the six hours from the time people arise from bed. I say that we rely on Raavyah, whom Beit Yosef cites from Mordechai at first, that it is permitted when one is studying or praying. Similarly, Agur siman 401 cites as practical law only the beginning of Mordechai's words. I likewise found in the manuscript Mordechai Katan, and further in Gedulat Mordechai, that even Mordechai's final ruling like Rabbi Yehoshua applies to Yom Tov, while on Shabbos one may extend beyond midday. This also resolves the apparent contradiction in Raavyah. This seems to accord with the view of Mordechai Katan and Agur mentioned above. It is therefore surprising that the Shulchan Aruch ruled otherwise. I later saw that Bach in siman 242 also rules this way, contradicting what he wrote here, which is even more surprising. See siman 242, seif katan 6.
[3] [Levush] And whenever, etc. In Shibbolei HaLeket and Tanya, the source of this rule concerns the third meal, so it must be understood as not necessarily limited to that case, in order to permit, etc. Thus Rama explains the account that Rabbi Akiva would weep and say, "This is a delight for me." Taz objects and wonders that according to this, anyone who is distressed should weep on Shabbos, God forbid. He therefore explains that Rabbi Akiva's tears came from the intensity of his attachment to the Holy One, blessed is He. Thus we find in Zohar Chadash that Rabbi Akiva wept greatly when reciting Shir HaShirim because he understood the lofty matters to which the words reached. This is likewise common among those who pray with concentration. I found, however, in Responsa Binyamin Ze'ev, siman 210, that the incident cited by the Agudah concerned Rabbi Akiva weeping over the death of Rabbi Eliezer. Rama's explanation is therefore correct. Moreover, Rashi on Ta'anit 12a explains that a dream fast is permitted so that the person's bodily distress will be relieved, as stated in seif 3. The objection that everyone who is distressed should therefore weep is not compelling, because it is not the nature of every person for distress to leave his heart through crying, and it also depends on the nature of the distress. The heart knows its own bitterness, and if one seeks to act deceptively, etc.

turei_zahav.he: וכן מי שיש לו עונג כו'. דאיתא באגדה שמצאו תלמידיו של רע"ק שהיה בוכה בשבת ואמר עונג יש לי ונ"ל דהיינו שמרוב דבקותו בהקב"ה זולגי' עיניו דמעו' שכן מצינו ברע"ק בזוהר חדש שהיה בוכה מאוד באמרו שיר השירים באשר ידע היכן הדברים מגיעים וכ"ה מצוי במתפללים בכוונה אבל כדי שיצא הצער ממנו שזכר רמ"א הוא תמוה דא"כ כל מי שמצטער ח"ו יבכה בשבת:
turei_zahav.en: And likewise one who has pleasure, etc., as stated in the Aggadah that they found the disciples of R' Akiva weeping on Shabbat and he said 'I have pleasure.' And it appears this means from his great cleaving to Heaven his eyes pour tears, as we find with R' Akiva in Zohar Chadash when saying Shir HaShirim he wept greatly because he knew where the matters reach; and likewise among those who pray with kavanah. But in order that sorrow leave him when he remembered — Rama — it is puzzling; if so:

mechaber.he: אדם המתענה בכל יום ואכילה בשבת צער הוא לו מפני שינוי וסת (פי' דבר קבוע) יש אומרים שראו כמה חסידים ואנשי מעשה שהתענו בשבת מטעם זה וכן אמרו שכך היה עושה ה"ר יהודה החסיד:
mechaber.en: Regarding a person who fasts every day, and eating on Shabbat is painful for him because of the change in routine (explanation: a fixed thing), some say they have seen many pious and noble people who have fasted on Shabbat because of this reasoning, and they say that so acted Rabbi Yehuda heChasid.

beur_hagra.he:
ס"ג אדם. וכן מ' בפ"ו דפסחים מר בריה דרבינא הוה ציים כו':
י"א כו'. ע' סי' קסז ס"כ אפי' כו' ועמ"א שם ס"ק מא כ"מ בגמ' כו' וטעמא כו':
beur_hagra.en:
(א) SJ of man. And Heaven’s Word is the same as Heaven’s Word:

(ב) (11) etc. See siman 167 seif 20 — even, etc.; and Magen Avraham there s.k. 41 as in the Gemara, etc., and the reason, etc.:

biur_halacha.he: צער הוא לו וכו' - ר"ל אפילו אם יאכל מעט דאל"ה אין לו למנוע מחמת זה:
biur_halacha.en: The sorrow is to him, and so on, even if he eats a little Dahl, he does not prevent this gift:

eliyah_rabbah.he:
[ד] ואכילה וכו'. אבל כשאין לו צער אף שמתענה על עוונות ומחמת תשובה אסור (בית יוסף ושיירי כנסת הגדולה), וכל שכן שאין לבעל תשובה לבכות מחמת תשובה (של"ה):
[ה] [לבוש] חלומו שראה וכו'. משמע אם חבירו ראה עליו אין מתענין וכן כתב שיירי כנסת הגדולה ובחול מתענין, והוא הדין כשחולם לעצמו מהפסד ממון, מיהו אם הוא דבר שמחללין עליו שבת כתב ספר חסידים תתס"ח דמתענין בשבת. כתב מגן אברהם סימן ר"כ בשם ספר חסידים מי שיחלום לו חלום קשה על חבירו יתענה עד כאן ופשוט דבשבת אין צריך:
[ו] [לבוש] שבעים שנה וכו'. כלומר אפילו נגזר עליו מנעוריו (רש"י ברכות ל"א), ונקט שבעים לפי שימי שנותינו שבעים שנה ועיין ב"ח, ובזוהר פרשת אמור פירש אינון שבעים כתרא מלכא דאסכימו עליה לרעה חס ושלום, עד כאן, ומשמע ברש"י שם דוקא בשבת שתענית קשה שהכל מתענגים והוא מתענה וכן כתב ראב"ן סימן קע"ט, ומלבוש משמע לכאורה דאף בחול קורעין וצריך עיון: וכן צריך לעסוק כל היום בתורה ויתכפר לו ומותר להתוודות על חטאיו כשמתענה כמו בחול (סדר היום), ומשמע משל"ה דף קל"א דמותר אפילו לבכות:
eliyah_rabbah.en:
[4] And eating, etc. If he has no distress, then even if he fasts for his sins and as an act of repentance, it is prohibited (Beit Yosef; Shiyurei Knesset HaGedolah). All the more so, a penitent should not weep on Shabbos because of his repentance (Shelah).
[5] [Levush] The dream that he saw, etc. This implies that if his fellow dreamed something about him, he does not fast, and Shiyurei Knesset HaGedolah writes likewise. On a weekday, however, he does fast. The same applies when one dreams of monetary loss concerning himself. Nevertheless, if the dream concerns something for which Shabbos may be desecrated, Sefer Chasidim 868 writes that one fasts even on Shabbos. Magen Avraham in siman 220 cites Sefer Chasidim that one who dreams a troubling dream about his fellow should fast. It is obvious that on Shabbos he need not do so.
[6] [Levush] Seventy years, etc. Meaning, even if the decree was issued against him in his youth (Rashi, Berachot 31b). Seventy is mentioned because "the days of our years are seventy years." See Bach. Zohar, parashat Emor, explains that these are the seventy royal crowns that agreed upon evil against him, God forbid. Rashi there implies that this tearing of the decree applies specifically to Shabbos, when fasting is particularly difficult because everyone else delights while he fasts. Raavan siman 179 writes likewise. Levush, however, appears to imply that this applies even on a weekday, which requires study. He should also occupy himself with Torah throughout the day and thereby obtain atonement, and he may confess his sins while fasting just as on a weekday (Seder HaYom). Shelah, p. 131, implies that he may even cry.

machatzit_hashekel.he:
(ס"ק ג) ביום כו' ובש"ג כו' ומדמה לה למ"ש סי' תקס"ח סי"א שכתב דהנודר להתענות סכום ימים ואירע בהם תענית חובה ה"ז עולה לו:
וכ"מ סס"י תקצ"ז כצ"ל שכ' שם המתענה תענית חלום בראש השנה אינו צריך למיתב תענית לתעניתו כיון דיש אומרים דמצוה להתענות בר"ה ול"ל האי טעמא. ת"ל הלא אחר ר"ה מיד צם צום גדליה אע"כ תענית חובה אינו עולה:
וכן יש להורות כמ"ש מ"ב והט"ז פסק כש"ג ודחה ראיית מ"א ע"ש וסיים וז"ל ולפי הסברא נרא' דאחר יה"כ א"צ תענית לתעני' שבת אפי' לא התענ' ביה"כ מחמת אונס ויה"כ מכפר על עשה ול"ת שעבר ובודאי חייב ע"ז כמו תעניתי' ויה"כ מכפר כ"ש בזה עכ"ל:
machatzit_hashekel.en:
(א) (c) On the day of the day of the day of the day, and in the morning, he was taught to the S.J.C., that he had written a lot of days, and that it was not for him:

(ב) And as a result of Heaven’s promise, Heaven’s promise is not to be able to do so in His Word And to the island of Tama. The non-observation of Heaven’s Word is not a blessing:

(ג) And likewise one should rule as Mishna Berurah and Taz ruled like Shiltai Gibborim and rejected Magen Avraham's proof, see there; and he concluded: and according to reasoning it appears after Yom Kippur one need not a fast for his Shabbat fast even if he did not fast on Yom Kippur from coercion — and Yom Kippur atones for positive and negative commandments he transgressed; and certainly he is obligated for this like his fasts; and Yom Kippur atones all the more in this — end of his words:

mishnah_berurah.he: (ה) ואכילה וכו' - אבל כשאין לו צער אף שמתענה על עונות ומחמת תשובה אסור:
mishnah_berurah.en: (h) And eating, and so on, but when he has no sorrow, he will answer the seasons and answer is forbidden:

peri_megadim.he:
מותר עט״ז עב״ח מזה. ומ״ש מענין ת״ח ולמחרתו י״ז בתמוז יע״ש עמ״א אות ג׳ בזה ואפילו נדר להתענות כך ימים והתענה ת״ח בשבת אין עולה הימים לשבת למ״א ועא״ר זיי״ן משמע שם דאם התענה ב׳ שבתות או ב׳ י״ט למ״ד דת״צ עולה ה״ה דיום אחד עולה לשניהן ולמ״ד ת״צ אין עולה ה״ה דתענית א׳ אין עולה לשתיהן יע״ש ופשוט די״ט שחל בשבת והתענה די ביום א׳. חלום בת״צ עולה לו א״ר זיי״ן בשם ע״ת. עמ״א תקס״ד אות א׳ ובשם של״ה דמשחלם בלילה אסור שוב לאכול ולשתות בלילה וא״ר יו״ד צידד בזה יע״ש:
אם ישן ליל שבת קודם אכילה וחלם לו ועמד יש להסתפק איך יעשה בקידוש דקיי״ל ברע״ג ס״א אין קידוש אלא במקום סעודה ואף אם אחרים אוכלים ושותים מ״מ מי שאין אוכל במקום סעודה הוא לא יצא ידי קידוש כבסימן רע״ג בט״ז אות ב׳ דאמר רבה לאביי טעימו כאן אע״ג דרבה מקדש ואכל שם הם לא יצאו בשמיעה זו אם לא אכלו שם א״כ למ״ד קידוש היום בכוס ד״ת כנראה מט״ז רע״א אות י״ט איך יבטל מקידוש היום ועמ״א א׳ שם ומיהו עונג שבת להתענות י״א ג״כ דהוי ד״ת מ״מ י״ל זה עונג לו משא״כ לבטל ק״ה ד״ת מפני ת״ח לא יתכן וגם בא״ר יו״ד צידד בזה די״ל בלילה רשאי לאכול. ואם קידש ולא אכל אף מ״ה לא יצא כנראה מתו׳ סוכה ג׳ וברכות י״א אלו היית נוהג כן לא קיימת מצות סוכה מימיך ובפתיחה כוללת אי״ה יבואר. ועמ״א תקצ״ז אות ג׳ ויראה דה״פ מהר״ם התענה וקידש קידושא רבה פ״ה על הכוס בשחרית ונתן לאחר לטעום אע״ג דאין קידוש אלא במקום סעודה אף בשחרית מ״מ מ״ה יצא ידי קידוש אף בלא סעודה וסובר דכל היכא דא״א יצא מ״ה עכ״פ ושעת הדחק הוה וע״ז כתב המ״א דקידושא רבה קיי״ל דרבנן משמע מתשובת מהר״ם דאי הוי ד״ת אין יוצא במ״ש בתפלה ועמ״א רע״א וזה שהראה שם לרס״י רע״א ואי״ה שם יבואר עוד בזה. וכאן אין להאריך ע׳ סוף הסי׳:
peri_megadim.en:
(א) Permitted — Taz; Av Beit Din from this. And what he wrote regarding the matter of a fast and the next day 17 Tammuz, see there Magen Avraham letter 3 on this; and even if he vowed to fast such days and fasted a fast on Shabbat — the days do not count toward Shabbat per Magen Avraham; and Eliyahu Rabbah letter 7 implies there that if he fasted two Shabbatot or two Yom Tov days — some say a public fast counts likewise one day counts for both; and per some a public fast does not count likewise one fast does not count for both, see there; and it is simple that Yom Tov that falls on Shabbat and he fasted — suffices on day one. A dream on a public fast counts for him — Eliyahu Rabbah letter 7 in the name of Orchot Chayim. Magen Avraham 564 letter 1; and in the name of Shelah that if he dreamed at night it is forbidden again to eat and drink at night; and Eliyahu Rabbah letter 10 sided on this, see there:

(ב) If he slept Shabbat night before eating and dreamed and arose — there is to be uncertain how he does Kiddush — for we hold in siman 273 seif 1 there is no Kiddush except in a place of a meal; and even if others eat and drink — nevertheless one who does not eat in a place of a meal does not fulfill Kiddush as siman 273 paragraph 16 letter 2 — for Rava said to Abaye "taste here" even though Rava sanctified and ate there they did not fulfill with this hearing if they did not eat there; if so per the view Kiddush of the day is in a cup d'oraisa as Taz 271 letter 19 implies — how does he nullify Kiddush of the day? Magen Avraham letter 1 there; nevertheless Shabbat pleasure to fast — some say likewise it is d'oraisa; nevertheless it may be said this is pleasure for him unlike nullifying one hundred blessings d'oraisa because of a fast — it cannot be; and Eliyahu Rabbah letter 10 also sided that at night he may eat. And if he sanctified and did not eat — in any case he did not fulfill as appears from Tosafot Sukkah 3 and Berachot 11 — "if you were accustomed so you did not fulfill the mitzvah of sukkah all your days"; and in the opening it includes Eliyahu Rabbah will be explained. Magen Avraham 597 letter 3 — and it appears here Maharam fasted and sanctified Kiddusha Rabba paragraph 5 on the cup in the morning and gave another to taste even though there is no Kiddush except in a place of a meal — even in the morning nevertheless he fulfilled Kiddush even without a meal; and he holds wherever if unavoidable he fulfills in any case; and it was a time of pressure; and on this Magen Avraham wrote Kiddusha Rabba we hold is rabbinic — it implies from responsum of Maharam that if it were d'oraisa one does not fulfill with what is said in prayer; Magen Avraham 271 and this that he showed there to Rashi 271 and Eliyahu Rabbah there will be explained further on this. And here one should not extend — see end of the siman:

mechaber.he: מותר להתענות בו תענית חלום כדי שיקרע גזר דינו וצריך להתענות ביום ראשון כדי שיתכפר לו מה שביטל עונג שבת ואם תשש כחו ואינו יכול להתענות שני ימים רצופים לא יתענה ביום ראשון ויתענה אח"כ: הגה וכ"ש אם היה ביום ראשון חנוכה או פורים או יו"ט אפי' יו"ט שני של גליות שאין להתענות עד אח"כ. יש אומרים מי שישן שינת צהרים וחלם לו חלום רע יתענה מחצי היום עד חצי הלילה ואז יבדיל וביום הראשון יתענה כאלו התענה כל יום השבת (מצאתי כתוב):
mechaber.en: It is permitted to fast the fast of a disturbing dream on Shabbat, in order that the decree of judgement may be torn up -- and they need to fast on Sunday, in order to atone for nullifying the delight of Shabbat. And if their strength is weakened and they can't fast two consecutive days, they don't have to fast on Sunday and should fast after that. {Rama: Rema: Also, if Sunday is Chanukah or Purim or a festival, even the second day of a festival in the Diaspora, one shouldn't fast until after then. Some say, one who had a nap in the middle of the day and dreamt a bad dream should fast from noon to midnight and then make havdalah, and fast on Sunday -- it's as though that person fasted the whole day of Shabbat. (I found it written)}

ateret_zekenim.he: וצריך להתענות כו' וי"א שאין לשנות המנהג רק יתענה ביום א' כו' (רש"ל בהגהות):
ateret_zekenim.en: And it should be said that the Torah should not only be changed on the day of the day

baer_heitev.he:
תענית חלום. ואם חבירו ראה עליו חלום רע אין להתענות בשבת שכנה"ג ע"ל סי' ר"ך. ויבלה כל היום בתורה ובתפלה ויוכל לומר חטאתי עויתי פשעתי. סדה"י. כתב הט"ז דאם הרהר ביום וחלם בלילה אין לו להתענות בשבת ע"ש ועיין בתשובות חינוך בית יהודה סי' ג' ובשבות יעקב סי' ל"ד:
ביום ראשון. ואם ביום ראשון הוא תענית חובה צריך להתענות יום אחר מ"ב סי' צ"ג ובש"ג פ"ג דשבועות כתב דא"צ תענית אחר. ויש להורות כמ"ש המ"ב וכן פסק הע"ת וכ"מ בסי' תקס"ח ס"ה ע"ש. וכנה"ג פסק כהש"ג מטעם ספק נפשות להקל וכ"פ הט"ז ע"ש שכתב דאפילו אם התענה בעי"כ א"צ למיתב תענית לתעניתו אפי' לא התענה בי"כ מחמת אונס ועיין בס' הלכה ברורה מה שהשיג עליו. ובתשובת שבות יעקב ח"ב סי' ט' הליץ בעדו ע"ש. ונ"ל דאם יום ראשון הוא יום ראשון של סליחות עולה לו לד"ה אם אינו רגיל להתענות כל שנה דהא אינו חובה כמ"ש סי' תקפ"א. אבל מי שיש לו מנהג להתענות ביום ראשון צריך להתענות תענית לתעניתו ביום אחר. מ"א ועיין בשכנה"ג:
חנוכה. אבל שאר ימים שאין מתענין בהם כגון יומי דניסן או סיון או א"ח יש להתענות בהם וה"ה בין יוה"כ לסוכות כנה"ג בשם הר"ש הלוי סי' ד' ובדרישה העתיק בשם רמ"א דביום שאין אומרים תחנון אין מתענין ובר"ח ניסן וה"ה ר"ח אב מתענין עי' סי' תקע"ג וסימן תק"פ וה"ה בע"פ. מ"א. ולענין כשמתענין באותן הימים על תענית חלום ודאי לא בעי למיתב תענית לתעניתו אבל בח"ה וי"ט שני צריך למיתב תענית לתעניתו. שכנה"ג ע"ש וכ"כ ע"ת:
היום. ואינו מתפלל עננו עי' סי' תקס"ב. מ"א. ובחול בכה"ג א"צ להתענות. מצאתי:
baer_heitev.en:
(א) Fast for a dream. And if his friend saw a bad dream about him, he should not fast on Shabbat, as Knesset HaGedolah wrote above siman 220. And he should spend the entire day in Torah and prayer and may say 'I have sinned, I have transgressed, I have acted wickedly.' Sedei Chemed. Taz wrote that if he contemplated during the day and dreamed at night, he should not fast on Shabbat, see there; and see responsa Chinuch Beit Yehudah siman 3 and Shevut Yaakov siman 34:

(ב) On Sunday. And if on Sunday, it is a mandatory answer that should be answered another day from C.C. and in the P.J., another lawyer wrote. It has to be It is as a result of Heaven’s Word and Heaven’s Word. the Gemara says that it is written in accordance there’s Word, and that Heaven’s Word is revealed to them He answered the congregation to respond to his pleasurable plea that he did not respond to such a pleasurable rape, and to see Bj as clear as he had achieved it. The answer is that Jacob is in the house . . . . . . . N. D.M. Sunday is the first day of forgiveness that rises to him if he is not accustomed to complaining each year, Dea is not mandatory As the S.C. [7] [Levush] Nevertheless he must, etc. If Sunday is a communal fast, Shiltei Gibborim is lenient in an inadvertent case and holds that it counts. Responsa Mas'at Binyamin, siman 93, rules that it does not count and that he must fast another day. He proves this from Terumat HaDeshen, siman 278, which states that one who observes a dream fast on Rosh Hashanah need not fast an additional fast for having fasted on the festival because some hold that it is a mitzvah to fast on Rosh Hashanah. This implies that otherwise an additional fast would be required and Tzom Gedaliah would not suffice. Olat Tamid and Magen Avraham rule likewise. Taz objects and gives two answers. First, the case of Rosh Hashanah may concern one who did not fast on Tzom Gedaliah because of circumstances beyond his control. Second, the purpose of the compensatory fast is that he intend it as atonement and be moved to repentance, so the requirement means that on Tzom Gedaliah he should intend that the fast serve as atonement. In my humble opinion, Taz did not see Terumat HaDeshen itself, for it states that he saw many people who fasted on Rosh Hashanah and none observed an additional compensatory fast, apparently because fasting on Rosh Hashanah is itself a mitzvah. The first answer is therefore difficult, for it is implausible that all of them failed to fast on Tzom Gedaliah because of unavoidable circumstances. The second is also difficult, since perhaps they did intend Tzom Gedaliah for atonement. The clear proof Taz cites from Yoreh Deah, end of siman 217, also appears below in siman 568, seif 11, but in truth it is no proof, as Magen Avraham writes, because here atonement is required, and we do not find atonement obtained without cost. I also examined Shiltei Gibborim itself and found that it remains in doubt for this very reason. I heard an objection to Mas'at Binyamin: perhaps Terumat HaDeshen needed the reason that fasting on Rosh Hashanah is a mitzvah because if one fasted both days of Rosh Hashanah, how could Tzom Gedaliah compensate for both? It appears to me that if a communal fast counts, then one fast can likewise compensate for fasting both days. Furthermore, Terumat HaDeshen itself asks whether a fast during the Ten Days of Repentance counts, since he fasts then in any event. This implies a case in which he fasted throughout the Ten Days of Repentance, yet it still invokes the reason that fasting on Rosh Hashanah is a mitzvah. We therefore learn that none of the Ten Days of Repentance count for one whose practice is to fast on them, contrary to Olat Tamid, who writes that days a person voluntarily accepts as fasts, such as the Ten Days of Repentance, do count. Terumat HaDeshen does not imply this. This also supports Magen Avraham's ruling that one whose custom is to fast on the first day of Selichot cannot count that day. If one has a bad dream on a communal fast, Olat Tamid rules that the communal fast counts for him.
[8] [Levush] And it is proper to fast, etc. So that he not delay seeking mercy and forgiveness (Rashba). Piskei Recanati, siman 178, states that the preferred fulfillment is on Sunday, for then it is evident that he fasts because of Shabbos. Although Shulchan Aruch uses the expression "must," Levush writes "it is proper," because Rashba himself in the chapter Ein Omdin writes that it is not an absolute obligation. Therefore, when Levush says "if his strength is weakened," it means even if his strength is only somewhat weakened. So it appears to me.
[9] Chanukah, etc. This implies specifically these days, but during Nisan, Sivan, and Isru Chag one may fast, as Rabbi Shlomo HaLevi writes. The same applies between Yom Kippur and Sukkot. Magen Avraham adds that even if Sunday is Rosh Chodesh Nisan, Rosh Chodesh Av, or Erev Pesach, he fasts. Perishah, however, quotes Rama as saying that one does not fast on a day when Tachanun is omitted. It is proper to rely on this, since Chiddushei Rashba cites an opinion that a dream fast does not require a compensatory fast at all, because the Gemara refers to one who voluntarily accepted a fast on Shabbos. Responsa Binyamin Ze'ev writes similarly. Although Rashba there and Rivash siman 513 write that most authorities disagree, nevertheless many authorities also hold that he need not fast specifically on Sunday, and even according to Rashba it is not an absolute obligation. Therefore, one should not fast on a day when Tachanun is omitted. See the end of siman 420 regarding my objection to Magen Avraham. Nevertheless, if one actually observes a dream fast on such days, even on Rosh Chodesh Nisan or Av, he need not observe a compensatory fast for having fasted then. The law of Erev Yom Kippur will be explained in siman 568, seif 5. The fifteenth of Av and the fifteenth of Shevat require study below.
[10] Until midnight, etc. The sermons of Maharam of Rothenburg state only until nightfall, and write that he must fast on Sunday because there is an opinion that one who completes a fast on Erev Shabbos until nightfall requires a compensatory fast (Malbushei Yom Tov). It appears to me that one may rely on this on the first day of Yom Tov, or when Yom Tov follows Shabbos on Sunday, or on the second day of Yom Tov when it falls on Friday, and then he need fast only until nightfall. It also appears so regarding one whose practice is to fast even on Shabbos and who has such a dream in the afternoon. Although it is possible that a person who was already fasting does not obtain the benefit of a dream fast, it appears to me that he is not obligated to observe a compensatory fast, because he did not thereby cancel Shabbos delight, since his practice is to fast. Shelah, p. 200, writes that if one dreams a troubling dream even in the middle of the night, he should taste nothing thereafter. It is not sufficient to begin fasting at dawn as on other fasts. He proves this from one who sleeps in the afternoon, who begins fasting immediately. It also appears to him that the man should separate from his wife, even on Shabbos when it is the prescribed time for marital relations, for if fasting and canceling Shabbos delight were permitted, this is all the more so. Magen Avraham in siman 564 writes likewise. In my humble opinion, however, one can distinguish between afternoon sleep during the day and nighttime sleep. There is some proof from those who observe a dream fast on both days of Rosh Hashanah but do not fast at night. Magen Avraham in siman 596 also writes that in a dream the matter was shown to him by day and not by night. It likewise appears possible to distinguish between a fast, which concerns him personally, and the mitzvah of marital relations, which he owes to his wife.

turei_zahav.en: (4) Permitted to fast on it a fast. Tur wrote the reason: this is pleasure for him that he thinks the fast will tear his decree — his soul is aggrieved over what he saw and he thinks it will be nullified through the reward of the fast — and such is the truth. And I say from what Tur wrote siman 568 in the name of Ra'avan and R' Chaim that one does not fast on Shabbat a fast in our time — because we are not expert in interpreting dreams; here it refers to Talmudic words when they were expert; and further it appears and this is primary that here it deals even in our time; and that which is forbidden below is from the side of law that a person thinks he is obligated to fast since Heaven showed him evil, Heaven forbid — therefore it is not so because we are not expert; therefore there is no obligation from the side of law; but here it deals from the side that he worries and is distressed even though he is uncertain in interpretation — nevertheless he worries about the uncertainty and fasts to nullify the uncertainty — this is pleasure for him and permitted. And accordingly it appears to me to distinguish in this ruling: if he dreamed one of the dreams mentioned here and afterward fasts — then even though he does not worry so much and his soul is not aggrieved over it, he fasts; and for other dreams where he is uncertain in their interpretation — we do not instruct him to fast unless his soul is aggrieved over it — then he has pleasure from this; and therefore Tur mentioned here "his soul is aggrieved"; and likewise siman 128; and further it appears that in every case where he thought during the day and it came to him in a dream afterward — there is no relevance to "Heaven showed him" — rather the thought causes it; and like the incident in the chapter "The Seer" — Shapur the king said to Shmuel: you say much wisdom — tell me what I saw in a dream — meaning the coming night; and he said: you saw Romans come and enslave you and grind you with golden millstones — he thought all day and saw — behold the matter depends on thought and there is no ruling from Heaven; therefore he should not fast on Shabbat for this, as is my primary view for practice: it is written in Mishna Berurah siman 293 in Taz Taz on Shabbat and the next day 17 Tammuz that one must fast after 17 Tammuz for what he fasted on Shabbat and 17 Tammuz does not help for this; and proof from Tosefta siman 248 who wrote: one who fasts a fast on Rosh Hashanah need not sit a fast for his fast — for some say it is a mitzvah to fast on Rosh Hashanah; it implies if not so a fast is required and the Fast of Gedaliah does not suffice; and likewise in Beit Yosef Orach Chayyim siman 568: one who fasts on Yom Kippur needs a fast for his fast — behold even Yom Kippur does not help — a fortiori 17 Tammuz; but in my humble opinion thus he learned this from the implication of the words of Tosefta and Beit Yosef; and if they intended for this they should have brought proof that it is so; and on the contrary it appears clear proof to the contrary from what Maharil wrote in responsum siman 125: one who vows to fast a number of consecutive days and a obligatory fast occurs among them — it is simple he is released from it — for he accepted it to afflict himself; and they brought it in Shulchan Aruch in the gloss Yoreh De'ah siman 217 at its end; and he brings further proof there in responsum from Yisrael who fulfills eighteen days of festival joy with vows and donations — evidently even though he must bring peace offerings of vows nevertheless he fulfills festival joy and we do not say since he vowed he must pay peace offerings of festival joy; and if so likewise this fast he is obligated because of Shabbat — he is released through an obligatory fast — for there is no difference between obligation of fast and obligation of festival joy; and this is clear proof for what he learned from Tosefta and Beit Yosef — two responsa on the matter: one — they did not want to say only that there is prohibition in fasting on Rosh Hashanah and therefore one needs a fast afterward; and practical difference if it happened he did not fast on Yom Kippur or on the Fast of Gedaliah such as he had coercion — he is obligated to fast because of the Shabbat fast afterward; second — the essence of the fast is that he intend it be atonement for that matter for which he fasted and think repentance on it — and on this he says one needs a fast for his fast — meaning he should intend on the obligatory fast day that it be atonement for what he fasted on Shabbat; but certainly not for that obligatory fast does he ascend to atone for everything — in particular Yom Kippur; and according to reasoning it appears after Yom Kippur one need not a fast for his Shabbat fast even if he did not fast on Yom Kippur truly from coercion — for Yom Kippur atones for positive and negative commandments he transgressed; and certainly he is obligated for this like his fasts; and Yom Kippur atones all the more in this, as above — clear:
